paragraphs: An agent that acts from images can make poor decisions when an attacker changes what it sees. Existing defenses have appeared robust even against large input perturbations. This paper argues that some of this apparent protection comes from a weakness in the attacks used to test those defenses: limiting changes through pixel-distance constraints can leave the meaning of an image largely intact.

The authors introduce SHIFT, a diffusion-based attack that changes the semantic content of an observed state. It is policy-agnostic, meaning its design does not depend on a particular agent policy. Its generated observations aim to remain visually realistic and consistent with the observation history, making the altered scene less conspicuous while presenting a misleading state.

In the reported evaluations, SHIFT defeats existing defenses, including sophisticated ones, and outperforms earlier attacks while being more perceptually subtle. These findings show why resistance to pixel-constrained perturbations may provide an incomplete picture of robustness. The results motivate policies that can withstand realistic changes in what an observation appears to mean.
neurips-2025-diffusion-guided-adversaria.tldr: SHIFT uses diffusion to create realistic, semantically misleading observations that defeat existing reinforcement-learning defenses in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper compares how human brains and artificial vision networks represent natural images as processing moves through successive stages. The authors measure both linear and nonlinear dimensionality in human fMRI activity and network features. These complementary measurements examine the geometry of representations, allowing the comparison to go beyond whether the two systems recognize similar objects.

In the human ventral visual stream, both measurements increase along the hierarchy, consistent with the development of semantic and abstract representations. Most artificial networks show a similar increase in linear dimensionality only when their features are pooled. This makes the choice of feature readout consequential: different ways of extracting network representations can change the apparent agreement with brain activity.

The nonlinear measurements reveal a different pattern, with dimensionality collapsing in later network layers. The authors suggest that this compression may reduce flexibility in generalizing to abstract features, whereas brain representations retain greater dimensionality. They propose dimensionality alignment as a benchmark for vision models, framing the functional consequences as a possible explanation rather than an established causal result.
neurips-2025-dimensionality-mismatch-bet.tldr: Human visual representations and artificial networks diverge in nonlinear dimensionality, suggesting a possible obstacle to flexible visual generalization.

paragraphs: Optimal transport can be sensitive to noise, motivating formulations that relax how distributions must be matched. This paper studies two such problems in the semi-discrete setting. Partial transport minimizes the cost of moving a specified amount of mass, alpha. Robust transport instead modifies the objective using a total-variation penalty controlled by lambda.

The authors show that optimal solutions to both problems have a shared geometric representation: a restricted Laguerre diagram. This characterization also creates an algorithmic connection. A solver for either formulation can be adapted to solve the other with comparable precision, allowing algorithmic progress on one problem to carry over to its counterpart.

Building on this structure, the paper extends cost-scaling techniques and gives an algorithm computing the solution to log(1/epsilon) bits of precision in n^{O(d)} log(1/epsilon) time. Here n is the discrete support size and d is the dimension. It also gives an approximation algorithm taking n^{1+o(1)} epsilon^{-O(d)} time. These bounds expose different trade-offs between support size, dimension, and precision rather than providing a single uniformly inexpensive solver.
neurips-2025-efficient-algorithms-for-ro.tldr: A shared geometric characterization connects robust and partial semi-discrete optimal transport and enables new precision-sensitive algorithms.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent learning is commonly tuned to maximize teamwork in ideal simulations. This study asks whether that tuning also produces robustness, meaning stability under uncertainty, and resilience, meaning recovery after disruption. The authors conduct more than 82,620 experiments spanning four real-world environments, thirteen uncertainty types, and fifteen hyperparameters.

Under mild uncertainty, better cooperation tends to accompany greater robustness and resilience. That relationship weakens as disturbances grow, and outcomes depend on both the algorithm and the uncertainty involved. Protection also fails to transfer reliably across disturbance types or affected agents: handling action noise across a whole team does not imply handling observation noise affecting just one member.

The study finds that hyperparameter choices materially affect these properties. Parameter sharing, GAE, and PopArt can hurt robustness, while early stopping, higher critic learning rates, and Leaky ReLU consistently help in the reported experiments. Hyperparameter changes alone improve cooperation, robustness, and resilience across the tested backbones, with similar findings for robust MARL methods. The practical implication is that trustworthy cooperation requires evaluating disturbances directly, alongside ideal-condition performance.
neurips-2025-empirical-study-on-robustne.tldr: A large empirical study shows that cooperative performance alone does not reliably predict multi-agent robustness or recovery under stronger disturbances.

paragraphs: When training data contain incorrect labels, one common response is to select examples that appear trustworthy and train on that subset. Existing methods often judge success by how much they lower the fraction of incorrect labels. This paper argues that the remaining mistakes deserve closer attention because different mislabeled examples can have different effects on learning.

The authors identify a particularly harmful group: examples with incorrect supplied labels that the model nevertheless predicts correctly early in training. They call these Mislabeled Easy Examples. Their proposed method, Early Cutting, revisits an initially selected confident subset using the model at a later training stage. This recalibration aims to remove misleading early selections and filter out these harmful examples.

Experiments on CIFAR, WebVision, and full ImageNet-1k show improvements in both sample selection and model performance through reducing Mislabeled Easy Examples. The result shifts attention from simply counting label errors toward identifying which errors are especially damaging. It also supports revisiting early confidence judgments instead of treating an initial selection as permanently reliable.
neurips-2025-enhancing-sample-selection-.tldr: Early Cutting revisits early sample selections to remove particularly harmful mislabeled examples and improve learning with noisy labels.

paragraphs: Concept-based explanations describe a network using higher-level ideas instead of only its low-level features. However, concepts extracted from internal activations may not reflect the decisions the classifier actually makes. FACE addresses this mismatch by making agreement with the original model part of the concept-learning objective.

The method combines non-negative matrix factorization with a Kullback-Leibler divergence regularizer. Factorization provides a concept representation, while the regularizer encourages predictions from that representation to match the model's original predictions. Classifier supervision therefore helps determine which concepts are learned, rather than leaving concept discovery dependent solely on encoder activations. The goal is an explanation whose predictive behavior remains aligned with the system being explained.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees connecting lower KL divergence with bounded differences between predictive distributions, supporting faithful local linearity in concept space. Evaluations on ImageNet, COCO, and CelebA report better faithfulness and sparsity than existing methods. Together, these results support learning compact concept explanations with an explicit predictive-consistency requirement, so that understandable structure remains connected to model behavior.
neurips-2025-face-faithful-automatic-con.tldr: FACE learns concept explanations with classifier supervision and predictive-consistency regularization, improving reported faithfulness and sparsity.

paragraphs: Data attribution asks how individual training examples affect a model. Gradient-based approaches, including influence functions, can investigate that question without repeatedly retraining the model. Their expense often comes from computing and storing a separate gradient for each example, which creates a substantial obstacle as models grow.

GraSS tackles this bottleneck through gradient compression that explicitly exploits the inherent sparsity of per-sample gradients. The paper also introduces FactGraSS variants designed specifically for linear layers. The stated computational contribution is sub-linear space and time complexity. This targets the machinery needed to estimate influence, making the attribution computation more economical while seeking to retain the information relevant to each example's effect.

Across extensive experiments, the authors report substantial speed improvements while preserving data-influence fidelity. In particular, FactGraSS achieves up to 165% faster throughput on billion-scale models relative to previous state-of-the-art baselines. This is a best reported improvement rather than a uniform gain for every setting. The findings indicate that exploiting gradient structure can help make attribution practical at larger model scales.
neurips-2025-grass-scalable-data-attribu.tldr: GraSS compresses sparse per-example gradients to accelerate data attribution while preserving influence fidelity in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Language models trained with human feedback depend on examples of what people prefer. HelpSteer3-Preference contributes more than 40,000 human-annotated preference samples covering varied applications, including STEM, coding, and multilingual tasks. Its CC-BY-4.0 license makes the resource openly reusable under the license terms, addressing the need for broader and higher-quality public preference data.

The authors use the dataset to train reward models, which provide preference-based signals for evaluating model responses. Their reward models score 82.4% on RM-Bench and 73.7% on JudgeBench. The paper reports these as top results and describes an approximately ten-percentage-point improvement over the previously best-reported reward-model results.

The work also demonstrates training generative reward models and using the resulting reward models to align policy models through reinforcement learning from human feedback. Thus, the contribution includes both a dataset and demonstrations of its use in the alignment workflow. The benchmark findings provide evidence that the collected preferences can support strong reward modeling across the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-helpsteer3-preference-open-.tldr: HelpSteer3-Preference releases over 40,000 human preference samples and supports reward models with strong reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: This study compares ways to learn useful behavior from previously collected trajectories that lack rewards. It focuses on navigation and varies dataset quality, diversity, and environmental conditions. The central question is how reinforcement-learning methods compare with planning methods when agents must make use of this fixed, reward-free experience.

The reinforcement-learning side includes goal-conditioned and zero-shot approaches. For the control-based approach, the authors train a latent dynamics model using a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, or JEPA, and then use that learned model to plan actions. This places learning a representation of environmental dynamics at the center of action selection.

The experiments find that model-free reinforcement learning benefits most from abundant high-quality data. Planning with learned latent dynamics is more data-efficient and generalizes better to unseen layouts in the evaluated navigation tasks. It also matches leading model-free approaches in trajectory stitching, the ability to combine useful portions of recorded behavior. These findings support latent-model planning as a strong option when offline trajectories are suboptimal or agents must adapt across varied environments.
neurips-2025-learning-from-reward-free-o.tldr: In reward-free offline navigation experiments, latent-dynamics planning uses data efficiently and generalizes well to unfamiliar layouts.

paragraphs: Neural collapse is a symmetric organization of training examples' feature representations near a network's output. Although it has been observed empirically, earlier theoretical accounts often ignored data structure or considered only multilayer perceptrons. This paper extends the analysis to deep residual networks and transformers while explicitly accounting for the data.

The authors prove that global optima are approximately collapsed for the studied deep, regularized architectures with LayerNorm, trained using cross-entropy or mean-squared-error loss. The approximation becomes tighter as depth increases. The conclusion concerns global optima under the analyzed setup; its force comes from connecting a recognizable representation pattern to the solutions of a specified training problem.

The paper also gives a formal reduction from large-depth end-to-end ResNet or transformer training to an equivalent unconstrained features model. This supports using that simpler theoretical model beyond settings that disregard data structure. Experiments on vision and language datasets show increasingly prominent neural collapse with greater depth, providing empirical support for the theoretical relationship between architecture depth and representation geometry.
neurips-2025-neural-collapse-is-globally.tldr: For the analyzed regularized ResNets and transformers, global optima approach neural collapse more closely as network depth grows.

paragraphs: Visual anomaly detection needs both a scoring function and a rule that turns scores into decisions. SAC-BL combines a strong anomaly constraint network with a betting-like decision rule and controls the false discovery rate. This paper examines its false positive rate, an aspect that the authors identify as insufficiently investigated.

The analysis first establishes favorable behavior on abnormal data when scores belong to a generalized Gaussian-like distribution family and the number of test examples tends to infinity. The authors describe these distributional and sample-size conditions as overly restrictive for practical applications. They therefore turn to improving the decision rule for finite samples.

Their replacement introduces randomization into the betting-like algorithm, producing stochastic BL, or SBL. Combined with the existing SAC network, this yields SAC-SBL. The theoretical results show that the new method can attain a smaller false positive rate while retaining false discovery rate control. Experiments across multiple visual anomaly benchmarks also favor SAC-SBL over SAC-BL. The contribution demonstrates how revising the score-to-decision step can improve detection without centering the change on a new scoring network.
neurips-2025-on-the-sac-bl-algorithm-for.tldr: SAC-SBL randomizes SAC-BL's decision rule to improve false positive rates while preserving false discovery rate control.

paragraphs: Unlearning research faces two connected challenges: changing what a language model retains and determining whether the change actually achieved forgetting. Fragmented implementations and inconsistent evaluation make methods difficult to compare. OpenUnlearning supplies a standardized, extensible framework intended to bring both the methods and their measurements into a common benchmarking environment.

The framework integrates thirteen unlearning algorithms and sixteen evaluations across TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP. It also supports analysis of forgetting behavior using more than 450 publicly released checkpoints. This collection gives researchers a shared basis for examining methods across a broad evaluation suite, rather than assembling each comparison from separate implementations.

The authors additionally introduce a meta-evaluation benchmark that assesses the faithfulness and robustness of the evaluation metrics themselves. That step matters because a favorable score is useful only insofar as the measurement reliably reflects unlearning. Alongside comparative benchmarking of methods, the framework makes evaluation quality an explicit research target. Its stated contribution is infrastructure for more rigorous and reproducible unlearning research.
neurips-2025-openunlearning-accelerating.tldr: OpenUnlearning standardizes comparisons of language-model unlearning methods and adds a benchmark for evaluating the reliability of unlearning metrics.

paragraphs: State-space models offer efficient sequence processing but struggle with long-range dependencies. This paper argues that ordinary associative recall, where a model retrieves a value from a key alone, misses an important complication. Its proposed joint-recall task requires retrieving the value associated with a key in a specified context, making context part of the retrieval problem.

The authors prove that state-space models lack the expressiveness to solve multi-query joint recall with sub-quadratic computation. They then show that combining these models with Context-Dependent Sparse Attention provides the expressiveness needed to solve that task within sub-quadratic computation. The result ties an efficiency limitation to a particular retrieval requirement and identifies an architectural way to address it.

For natural-language use, the paper introduces HAX, which implements the proposed approach through locality-sensitive hashing attention and sparse key selection. On synthetic and real-world long-context benchmarks, HAX consistently outperforms the evaluated state-space baselines and hybrids using context-independent sparse attention. These results support selecting attention connections according to context as a useful addition to efficient state-space processing.
neurips-2025-overcoming-long-context-lim.tldr: HAX adds context-dependent sparse attention to state-space models, addressing a joint-recall expressiveness limit and improving tested long-context performance.

paragraphs: QCircuitBench evaluates whether AI can design and implement quantum algorithms as quantum circuit code. The paper frames this as a distinct challenge from ordinary code generation because quantum algorithm design has a highly flexible design space and requires precise handling of quantum states. It contributes a general framework for expressing these tasks for language models.

The dataset covers three task suites, twenty-five algorithms, and 120,290 data points, ranging from basic primitives to advanced applications. Automatic validation and verification functions support repeated, interactive evaluation without requiring human inspection. This makes checking generated implementations part of the benchmark, alongside the tasks that elicit them.

Experiments reveal recurring error patterns across model outputs, and fine-tuning does not always outperform few-shot learning. At the same time, results from primitive fine-tuning suggest that the dataset has promise as training material. These findings give the benchmark a dual role: measuring current capabilities and supporting work on improving them. They also show that additional training alone does not consistently resolve the tested quantum-programming challenges.
neurips-2025-qcircuitbench-a-large-scale.tldr: QCircuitBench provides automatically checked quantum-circuit tasks that expose recurring language-model errors and mixed benefits from fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Training language models with fewer bits can improve throughput and energy efficiency, but very low precision can damage accuracy. This paper studies hardware-supported FP4 training on NVIDIA Blackwell. It targets end-to-end training in which all major linear-layer computations use low precision, addressing approaches that lose substantial accuracy or rely on higher-precision fallbacks.

Through evaluations of Llama-type models, the authors derive a low-precision scaling law describing performance trade-offs across bit widths and training configurations. They use that investigation to design Quartet around the balance between accuracy and computation. The claim of optimality is tied to this accuracy-versus-computation objective and the investigated training setups.

Quartet is implemented with CUDA kernels optimized for Blackwell hardware. The reported results show that fully FP4-based training can be competitive with FP16 and FP8 training. The work therefore connects an empirical understanding of precision trade-offs with a hardware-specific implementation. Its significance is demonstrating a viable route to accurate low-precision training, rather than assuming that reducing numerical precision automatically produces a favorable training outcome.
neurips-2025-quartet-native-fp4-training.tldr: Quartet uses a low-precision scaling analysis and Blackwell-specific kernels to make native FP4 training competitive with FP16 and FP8.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a projection-free optimization method for objectives written as the difference of two convex functions. That class includes smooth nonconvex minimization. Its central opportunity is that the same objective can have multiple such decompositions, allowing the algorithm's formulation to reflect useful structure in the problem.

By choosing a decomposition carefully, the method can improve computational efficiency, adapt to the problem's geometry, and find better local solutions. The authors prove an O(1/epsilon²) iteration bound for reaching a first-order stationary point to the desired accuracy, matching the general complexity of standard Frank-Wolfe for smooth nonconvex minimization. This is a stationarity guarantee, with local solutions remaining central to the nonconvex setting.

Specific decompositions offer an additional benefit: a gradient-efficient variant needs only O(1/epsilon) gradient-oracle calls by reusing gradients across several iterations. This distinguishes the cost of obtaining gradients from the total iteration count. Numerical experiments support the method's effectiveness relative to other projection-free algorithms, showing why decomposition choice can matter even when the general iteration bound stays unchanged.
neurips-2025-revisiting-frank-wolfe-for-.tldr: A structured Frank-Wolfe method exploits convex-difference decompositions, matching standard stationarity complexity while enabling fewer gradient calls in specific cases.

paragraphs: This paper proposes incorporating safety into language-model pretraining through changes to the training data. Its motivation is that unsafe patterns learned early can be difficult to remove through later alignment. The framework therefore addresses how potentially harmful material is classified, presented, and marked while the model is learning.

The approach has four components. A safety classifier separates safe and unsafe web data. Rephrasing places unsafe material into safer narratives. Synthetic examples teach refusal of unsafe content together with moral reasoning. Finally, a special harmfulness token labels unsafe content during pretraining and is used to steer the model away from unsafe generation at inference time.

On the reported standard safety benchmarks, the safety-pretrained models reduce attack success rates from 38.8% to 8.4%, with no observed degradation on general tasks. These findings support the combined data-centric framework as a way to improve measured safety while maintaining evaluated capabilities. The contribution spans both learning-time data design and an inference-time steering mechanism, connecting the treatment of unsafe content during training with the model's later responses.
neurips-2025-safety-pretraining-toward-t.tldr: A four-part safety-pretraining framework lowers reported attack success from 38.8% to 8.4% without degrading evaluated general-task performance.

paragraphs: Language models often revisit proposed solutions, check them, and explore alternatives during reasoning. Yet their limited ability to detect mistakes leaves the benefit of this reflection unclear. The authors isolate the question in a minimal reasoning framework for small transformers that avoids natural language, making theoretical analysis and broad experimentation more manageable.

The paper proves that self-verifying reflection guarantees improvement when verification errors are appropriately bounded. Experiments show that transformers with only a few million parameters benefit from self-verification during both training and reflective execution. On integer multiplication and Sudoku, these small models reach performance the authors describe as comparable to that of large language models.

Reinforcement learning improves in-distribution performance and encourages more frequent reflection, but the experiments suggest it mainly captures shallow statistical patterns rather than faithfully reducing verification errors. This distinction matters because checking more often does not necessarily mean checking more accurately. The work supports combining generation with discriminative verification as a reasoning mechanism, while making clear that the theoretical improvement guarantee depends on the verifier's error bounds.
neurips-2025-self-verifying-reflection-h.tldr: Small-transformer experiments and conditional theory show how self-verification can improve reasoning, while frequent reflection need not mean more accurate checking.

paragraphs: Step-by-step reasoning can improve language-model performance, but generating lengthy explanations takes time. Implicit reasoning compresses those steps into hidden embeddings instead of explicit words. SemCoT addresses two weaknesses in existing approaches: compressed reasoning can lose the meaning of the reference reasoning, and each implicit token can still be expensive to generate.

The framework trains a sentence transformer contrastively to assess semantic agreement between implicit reasoning and explicit reference reasoning. This assessment guides optimization so that compression preserves meaning. SemCoT also distills reasoning into a lightweight language model, which generates the implicit tokens more efficiently while being trained for accuracy and semantic alignment.

The approach therefore targets both how much reasoning is represented and the time required to produce each implicit token. Reported experiments show better efficiency and effectiveness than state-of-the-art comparison methods. The contribution is a coordinated approach to reasoning compression: speed comes from a smaller generator, while a separate semantic signal helps keep the compressed computation connected to the intended reasoning.
neurips-2025-semcot-accelerating-chain-o.tldr: SemCoT accelerates implicit reasoning with a lightweight generator guided to preserve the meaning of explicit reference reasoning.

paragraphs: Surrogate models approximate complex systems so that scientific and engineering work can proceed at lower computational cost. The paper identifies a reporting problem across this field: choices about data sampling, model selection, evaluation, and downstream analysis are not consistently documented. That fragmentation makes results harder to reproduce and knowledge harder to transfer between domains.

The authors advocate a Surrogate Model Reporting Standard, or SMRS, to capture essential design and evaluation decisions in a structured way. The proposed direction remains independent of implementation details, so different modeling approaches can share a reporting framework. Its purpose is to make consequential choices visible without prescribing one technical method for building every surrogate.

The growth of AI-driven surrogate modeling makes this coordination increasingly pressing in the authors' argument. A standardized but flexible reporting approach is intended to improve reliability and interdisciplinary reuse, ultimately supporting scientific progress. These are the aims of a proposed reporting standard. The contribution is an argument for organizing and communicating modeling evidence more consistently across a fragmented field.
neurips-2025-smrs-advocating-a-unified-r.tldr: SMRS advocates flexible, standardized reporting of surrogate-model design and evaluation choices to improve reproducibility and cross-domain reuse.

paragraphs: Codebook-based image compression represents image tokens using entries from a learned collection. A single shared codebook can overlook differences between tokens and correlations associated with image categories. This paper focuses on faces, where those distinctions matter especially when very few bits are available to represent each pixel.

The proposed method learns separate codebook groups for different image categories and gives each token an independent codebook. A small number of extra bits records the group associated with each token. This identification overhead helps reduce the reconstruction loss caused by shrinking individual codebook groups, allowing a larger total collection of codebooks within a low overall bit budget.

The authors describe the design as compatible with existing codebook-based representation-learning approaches. On face-recognition datasets, reconstructed images achieve an average recognition accuracy of 93.51% at 0.05 bits per pixel. That result concerns recognition using reconstructed images, rather than exact recovery of every original pixel. It supports the claim that category-aware and token-specific coding can retain useful facial information under aggressive compression.
neurips-2025-switchable-token-specific-c.tldr: Category-aware, token-specific codebooks improve low-bit-rate face compression, with reported recognition accuracy of 93.51% at 0.05 bits per pixel.

paragraphs: Longer chains of thought can improve language-model reasoning, but this paper investigates whether extending them too far can become counterproductive. Experiments on mathematical reasoning find that longer reasoning can reduce performance in certain domains. The authors also find that the best distribution of reasoning lengths differs across domains, making uniform length expansion an imperfect strategy.

Their Thinking-Optimal Scaling method first uses a small seed dataset containing varied response-length distributions to teach different levels of reasoning effort. The model then tackles additional problems at different effort levels and selects its shortest correct response for self-improvement. This procedure uses correctness and brevity together to shape the reasoning examples learned from.

Models built on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct outperform other distillation-based 32B o1-like models across the reported math benchmarks. They also reach performance comparable to QwQ-32B-Preview, the teacher that supplied the seed data. These findings support learning how much reasoning to use, with successful shorter responses providing a training signal instead of treating longer output as inherently better.
neurips-2025-towards-thinking-optimal-sc.tldr: Thinking-Optimal Scaling trains models on their shortest correct responses after finding that excessive reasoning length can hurt some mathematical tasks.

paragraphs: Many physical models have a prescribed energy behavior: energy is either conserved or dissipated as the system evolves. Numerical simulations should respect that behavior as they approximate the underlying differential equations. This paper addresses the difficulty of choosing among numerous numerical methods that preserve such laws.

UEPI learns energy-behavior-preserving integrators from data, with the goal of obtaining high numerical accuracy while retaining the relevant conservation or dissipation property. The object being learned is the numerical integration method itself. This connects data-driven adaptation with a structural requirement supplied by the physical model, so accuracy and energy behavior are considered together.

The reported numerical studies find learned integrators more accurate than existing numerical methods across several differential equations, including chaotic Hamiltonian systems, dissipative systems, and a nonlinear partial differential equation. The authors also establish universal approximation theorems for their approach. The numerical findings demonstrate its performance on the tested systems, while the theorems supply complementary support for the expressive capacity of the proposed learning framework.
neurips-2025-uepi-universal-energy-behav.tldr: UEPI learns accurate numerical integrators from data while preserving the energy conservation or dissipation behavior of the modeled system.

paragraphs: LoRA adapts language models through low-rank weight updates, and several variants further reduce the number of trainable parameters. Uni-LoRA places these variants in a shared mathematical framework. It views all LoRA parameters as one large flattened vector reconstructed by projecting a much smaller trainable vector into that larger space.

Within this view, the choice of projection matrix distinguishes different methods. The authors argue that layer-specific or structure-specific projections restrict sharing across layers and compromise parameter efficiency. They introduce an isometric projection that enables global parameter sharing and reduces computational overhead. Their design reconstructs the entire model's LoRA parameters from a single trainable vector.

This makes Uni-LoRA both an interpretation of existing adaptation methods and a concrete adaptation technique. Experiments on GLUE, mathematical reasoning, and instruction tuning report state-of-the-art parameter efficiency while matching or exceeding earlier approaches in predictive performance. The findings suggest that the organization of parameter sharing across a model can be as consequential as reducing the number of adjustable parameters within individual layers.
neurips-2025-uni-lora-one-vector-is-all-.tldr: Uni-LoRA unifies compact LoRA variants through projections and introduces global sharing that reconstructs all LoRA parameters from one trainable vector.

paragraphs: Common-O Bench tests whether multimodal models can identify what different scenes have in common. It contains more than 10,500 examples built from new images absent from web training data, addressing contamination concerns. Inspired by human cognitive tests, it asks models to reason across scenes rather than only recognize objects within individual images.

The evaluated models generally handle single-image object perception well but struggle with cross-scene reasoning, including models explicitly trained to reason. The strongest reported result is 35% on Common-O Bench and only 1% on Common-O Complex, which uses more complicated scenes. This exposes a substantial gap between performance on perception-focused leaderboards and the benchmark's reasoning demands.

Models hallucinate more often when similar objects appear, suggesting possible reliance on object co-occurrence patterns learned during training. Larger scale provides modest gains among the evaluated models, while explicit multi-image training is associated with bigger improvements. The authors therefore identify scaled multi-image training as a promising direction, while the observed association does not establish a complete solution to cross-scene hallucination.
neurips-2025-whats-in-common-multimodal-.tldr: Common-O Bench reveals severe cross-scene reasoning failures in multimodal models despite strong single-image perception.
